years.title: The Brothers Karamazov
years.kicker: 2023 · The Brothers Karamazov · one big Russian novel
years.why: The starter misogi, before it had a name. One deliberately heavy book, that I felt like I was “supposed” to have read, and never did.

protocol.cadence: Whenever. Hard to get through, and didn’t realize it was the start of something bigger until after I was done.
protocol.route: Front to back, no shortcuts. Engage with the critics, force myself to talk to friends about it.
protocol.scaffolding: None! I listened to a few podcasts and found some critics afterwards. Realized I needed more upfront/during.
protocol.rules: Finish it, think critically about it and talk about it.

years.gave: Holy shit. This book is just about life.

years.title: The Bible
years.kicker: 2024 · The Bible · cover to cover · 366 days
years.why: The obvious one: the most-referenced book in the civilization I live in, and I had never read it straight through. I grew up Catholic. Familiar with the stories, but I wanted to see what really doing the work of reading it day in and day out would do for me.

protocol.cadence: Twenty minutes, every day, first thing before anyone else was up.
protocol.route: Genesis to Revelation in canonical order, without skipping, without summarizing, without glossing.
protocol.scaffolding: THe Bible Recap - Tara Leigh Cobble for daily narratives. Bible Project videos and Youtubes for book overviews. Bible for Normal People podcast for a 30k foot view.
protocol.rules: Twenty minutes a day. Specifically used NSV not King James for “easier” reading.

years.title: Jorge Luis Borges
years.kicker: 2025 · Jorge Luis Borges · the complete works
years.why: After the Bible's single long road, the opposite terrain: dozens of short, dense, perfect objects. And the first misogi where an AI reading partner became part of the method.

protocol.cadence: Short story format was fun, could choose based on how much time I had but generally 2-20 minutes daily.
protocol.scaffolding: AI as the standing reading partner, helping untangle the labyrinths, chasing the references, testing my readings against the text.
protocol.rules: No rules. Read all of Borges in any order you want.

years.gave: Reading Borges is like walking on a mobius strip or looking at a magic eye picture.

years.title: Shakespeare
years.kicker: 2026 · Shakespeare · the complete plays · in progress
years.why: Interior work with the whole canon: fathers and sons, control, the need to be right, anger, reconciliation. Coming off Borges and the Bible, the through-line stays the same. How does life work, what does it mean, what should we do.

protocol.cadence: Try for an Act a day, often times half an Act.
protocol.route: A deliberate ladder: early comedies to establish the habit, the Henriad in spring for the father/son masterclass, the great tragedies at the height of summer, the late romances to close. My personal theme: fathers reckoning with what they broke.
protocol.scaffolding: Folger editions with No Fear alongside. Not stressed about grappling with meaning, I will just look it up if i can’t get it.  Critics: Bloom , Garber when Bloom gets too eccentric, Greenblatt. The Folger podcast, Globe productions, a film after the big ones. And a dedicated AI conversation per play, or a reading partner that never tires of questions.
protocol.rules: Buffer days are built into every month. The schedule bends, but the mornings habit doesn’t.

plays.name: The Comedy of Errors
plays.note: Shortest play. Farcical. Warm-up.

plays.name: The Two Gentlemen of Verona
plays.note: Early, slight. Friendship vs. love.

plays.name: The Taming of the Shrew
plays.note: Problematic but psychologically interesting. Control dynamics.

plays.name: Love's Labour's Lost
plays.note: Dense wordplay. Youthful cleverness confronting mortality.

plays.name: A Midsummer Night's Dream
plays.note: First major comedy. Dreams, transformation, what we can't see in ourselves.
plays.verdict: The play-within-the-play is a tragedy played as comedy. Shakespeare showing you what this story could have been.

plays.name: Henry VI, Part 1
plays.note: Collaborative, episodic. France, Joan of Arc.

plays.name: Henry VI, Part 2
plays.note: York emerges. Political chaos.

plays.name: Henry VI, Part 3
plays.note: Brutality. Richard of Gloucester rises.

plays.name: Richard III
plays.note: First great villain study. Seduction and self-deception.

plays.name: King John
plays.note: Minor history. The Bastard Faulconbridge is interesting.

plays.name: The Merchant of Venice
plays.note: Control from beyond the grave. Shylock's complexity.

plays.name: Much Ado About Nothing
plays.note: Wit as defense mechanism.

plays.name: As You Like It
plays.note: The forest as transformative space.

plays.name: Twelfth Night
plays.note: Peak comedy. Feste's wisdom.

plays.name: Richard II
plays.note: The lyric king. Identity dissolved with the crown.

plays.name: Henry IV, Part 1
plays.note: Key play. Hal between two fathers.

plays.name: Henry IV, Part 2
plays.note: Deeper, sadder. “I know thee not, old man.”

plays.name: Henry V
plays.note: Hal becomes king. Propaganda and genuine heroism.

plays.name: The Merry Wives of Windsor
plays.note: Falstaff resurrected for comedy. Light.

plays.name: Julius Caesar
plays.note: Rhetoric and self-deception.

plays.name: Titus Andronicus
plays.note: The revenge-play template. Complete works means complete.

plays.name: Troilus and Cressida
plays.note: War as degradation. Anti-romantic.

plays.name: Measure for Measure
plays.note: Control, judgment, mercy. Who gets to judge?

plays.name: All's Well That Ends Well
plays.note: The uncomfortable resolution.

plays.name: Romeo and Juliet
plays.note: Young tragedy. The contrast for what comes next.

plays.name: Hamlet
plays.note: The mountain. The father/son play. Take your time.

plays.name: Othello
plays.note: Jealousy as self-destruction.

plays.name: King Lear
plays.note: Fathers and children. Giving up control. Madness as stripping away.

plays.name: Macbeth
plays.note: Ambition, guilt. Lady Macbeth as shadow.

plays.name: Antony and Cleopatra
plays.note: Grandeur and ruin. Middle-aged passion.

plays.name: Coriolanus
plays.note: The need to be right. Mother and son.

plays.name: Timon of Athens
plays.note: Rage after betrayal. Brief.

plays.name: Henry VIII
plays.note: Late pageantry. Katherine's dignity.

plays.name: The Two Noble Kinsmen
plays.note: Completist.

plays.name: Pericles
plays.note: First romance. The recognition scene is the template.

plays.name: Cymbeline
plays.note: Forgiveness despite nothing being earned.

plays.name: The Winter's Tale
plays.note: After you've broken it completely, is restoration possible?

plays.name: The Tempest
plays.note: Control, letting go. “Every third thought shall be my grave.” Read slowly.

principles: Pick one mountain, only one, a year.
Make it slightly too big; the point is that it doesn't fit inside casual effort.
Set a daily minimum dose and keep it small. Twenty minutes you do beats two hours you won't.
Scaffold shamelessly: podcasts, critic companions, film versions, AI. Anything that gives you momentum is not only allowed but encouraged.
Order the route around your seasons; save the summit for when you'll have the most capacity. Schedule in slack and use it when you need it.
Keep a log, but don’t go crazy. A checkbox a day is enough.
Let it end. December is for re-reading and reflection. If you’re moved or motivated to do more, you wont have to foce it.

intro.t: One deliberately oversized reading project a year. I pick it intentionally and make it a daily habit. I scaffold shamelessly, whatever keeps the momentum. A misogi is the one hard thing you do each year; this is my reading version. The point is as much having read it as
what the year spent reading it does to you.
